Forecast analysis

Forecast analysis

Probabilistic, not a prediction: built from historical base rates and current volatility. Overlapping 3-month windows mean the true sample is smaller than the day count.

Base case (next 1–3 months): range-bound with a coin-flip tilt. Signals disagree, which historically means choppier returns and more false breakouts. Let price confirm before committing new money. Over roughly 12 years of history, when the S&P 500 was in today's setup (uptrend, momentum rising), it was higher three months later 78% of the time (median move +4.4%), versus 78% in all conditions. Based on current volatility, a typical (~68% likely) 3-month range is $719–$803 from today's $760.

Key levels to watch on the S&P 500 (SPY): 50-day average $767, 200-day average $724. Price is between the two averages, a common zone for chop; direction out of it matters.

Warning flags: Small caps vs large caps, 3-mo change.

Supportive signals: S&P 500 vs 200-day average; 50-day vs 200-day average; Yield curve (10y − 2y); High-yield credit spread.

What would change this view: the S&P 500 closing below its 200-day average, the VIX holding above 25, high-yield spreads widening sharply, or breadth falling below 40% would shift the outlook toward risk-off.

Capital flow pressure

Capital flow pressure

Timeframe: Oct 23, 2025 – Oct 23, 2026 (254 trading days, the report period). Flow score (−1 to +1): of all the dollars traded in each asset's ETF over this period, the share traded on days the price closed up minus the share on days it closed down. +1 means every dollar traded on up days (steady buying), −1 means every dollar traded on down days (steady selling), and near 0 means balanced. It's an estimate from price and volume, not actual fund flows. Drag the slider or press ▶ Play to step through the past year: each step scores the month ending that week. Bars keep the same order and scale throughout; the "Report period" button returns to the full-period view.

Asset class flows, month by month

Each cell is one asset class's flow score for one calendar month (same −1 to +1 scale). Rows are in the same order as the chart above. Rotation shows up as color shifting between rows over time, for example a row turning red while another turns green.

The links show relative pressure, not literal dollar transfers from one asset to another.

Sector rotation

Typical cycle runs clockwise: Improving → Leading → Weakening → Lagging. Improving sectors are early rotation candidates.

Macro backdrop

Macro backdrop

Range buttons control all panels together. Click a line to open its source data. The M2 panel overlays the inflation rate (orange, right axis): money-supply surges have tended to show up in inflation roughly a year or more later.

Factor leadership

Momentum and high beta leading = risk appetite; min-vol and quality leading = defense.

Market breadth

Below 20% on the 50-day line has historically marked washed-out conditions; above 80% marks euphoria.

Cross-asset correlations

Low or negative correlations = real diversification. Watch for stocks and bonds moving together (both red together hurts 60/40).

Data sources

Data sources

  • Prices, volume, ownership, insider summaries, analyst targets: Yahoo Finance (via the open-source yfinance library). Every ticker in this report links to its Yahoo page.
  • Macro series (FRED, St. Louis Fed): T10Y2Y · T10Y3M · BAMLH0A0HYM2 · DFF · WALCL · M2SL · DTWEXBGS · CPIAUCSL
  • Company filings & insider trades: SEC EDGAR — Form 10-K/10-Q (financials) and Form 4 (insider buys/sells).
  • Institutional holdings (13F): SEC 13F overview
  • Congressional trades (optional): Quiver Quantitative
  • Stock universe: S&P 500 constituents (Wikipedia)
Method notes & limitations

Method notes & limitations

  • Capital flows are estimated from signed dollar volume on liquid ETFs (dollars traded on up days minus down days). True fund-flow data (ETF creations/redemptions, EPFR, 13F aggregates) is paid; this proxy tracks it reasonably but not perfectly.
  • Institutional ownership comes from 13F filings via Yahoo, which lag by up to ~45 days after each quarter.
  • “Public figures” = company insiders (officers/directors filing Form 4) and, optionally, members of Congress (STOCK Act disclosures via Quiver, which can lag up to 45 days).
  • Stock screen scores combine factors with published evidence: short-term reversal measured against the sector (Da, Liu & Schaumburg 2014), 12-month momentum (Jegadeesh & Titman 1993), the 52-week-high effect (George & Hwang 2004), Piotroski F-score (2000) and Altman Z-score (1968), estimate revisions (Chan, Jegadeesh & Lakonishok 1996), post-earnings drift (Bernard & Thomas 1989), insider purchases (Cohen, Malloy & Pomorski 2012), short interest (Asquith, Pathak & Ritter 2005) and lottery-like spikes (Bali, Cakici & Whitelaw 2011). The evidence comes from diversified portfolios held for months, and many of these effects have weakened since publication; the weights are judgment calls, not fitted values. Backtest before relying on them.
  • Oversold is not the same as cheap, and under-loved is not the same as undervalued. Trend filters separate dips in uptrends from falling knives, but no screen replaces reading the filings.
  • Forecasts are base rates from history plus current volatility. Markets change; past odds are a starting point for judgment, not a guarantee.
  • Backtest any rule before trusting it with money. Past relationships break, and free data has gaps.

This report is generated by a mechanical research tool and is not financial advice. Do your own due diligence and consider a licensed advisor for decisions about your money.
